item.title: AI Coding Agents in Practice: Claude Code, Copilot and Codex
item.description:
Part 2 of 2 · AI in my workflow
  1. Free Local Dictation That Works Everywhere
  2. AI Coding Agents in Practice: Claude Code, Copilot and Codex
TipTL;DR
  • Use VS Code with the agent’s extension. Its chat runs the same agent as the terminal.
  • Long tasks on a remote server: claude, copilot or codex in tmux, or Copilot’s chat with Session Target: Copilot.
  • Several tasks: one session each, in separate git worktrees.

Who leads

The eight most used tools in the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026, published in October 2026. The question: “Have you used any of the following coding agents or assistants in the past year?” 12,255 developers answered. Many use more than one tool, so the numbers add up to more than 100%.
Tool Used in the past year
Claude Code 65.5%
GitHub Copilot 58.7%
OpenAI Codex 29.5%
Cursor 25.5%
Google Antigravity 16.0%
Gemini Code Assist 14.6%
Open Code 13.6%
JetBrains AI 12.8%

What each company offers

The products in November 2026, as named by each company. In VS Code, Claude Code and Codex are extensions you install from the Marketplace, while GitHub Copilot Chat comes built in. All three desktop apps run on Windows, macOS and Linux (Claude on Linux is in beta).
Anthropic GitHub (Microsoft) OpenAI
Coding brand Claude Code GitHub Copilot Codex
Web chat claude.ai github.com/copilot chatgpt.com
Desktop app Claude GitHub Copilot ChatGPT
VS Code Claude Code for VS Code GitHub Copilot Chat Codex – OpenAI’s coding agent
Terminal claude copilot codex
Cloud agent Claude Code in the cloud Copilot cloud agent Codex Cloud
AI models Claude Claude, GPT, Gemini and others GPT

Which editor developers use

The eight most used editors in the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026. The question: “Which development environments and code editors did you use regularly over the past year?” 13,193 developers answered. Many use more than one editor, so the numbers add up to more than 100%.
Editor Used regularly
Visual Studio Code 70.9%
Notepad++ 27.8%
Visual Studio 27.6%
Vim 27.2%
IntelliJ IDEA 24.3%
Cursor 14.9%
Neovim 14.7%
Android Studio 14.2%

What “agent” means in practice

An agent is an AI that works on a task by itself, step by step. It reads files, edits code and runs commands, checks the result, and continues. In daily talk, “an agent” points to one of three concrete things:

From the official docs: VS Code sessions, Claude Code subagents, Copilot automations, Claude Code scheduled tasks, ChatGPT scheduled tasks, VS Code custom agents, Claude Agent SDK (“the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code”), GitHub Copilot SDK (“the same agent runtime behind GitHub Copilot”).
What it is What people say Examples
Session One running agent: a conversation in which the AI works on one task. You start it, a schedule starts it, or another session starts it (then it is called a subagent) “I use an agent for coding”, “I run four agents at once”, “My agents do this every morning”, “It started three subagents” A chat in the VS Code Chat view, a terminal window running claude, copilot or codex, a session in the desktop app. Started by a schedule: Copilot automations, Claude Code scheduled tasks, ChatGPT scheduled tasks
Custom agent A text file with a name, instructions and the tools the AI may use. Nothing runs. Sessions and subagents start from it “I created my first agent” .github/agents/reviewer.agent.md in VS Code, .claude/agents/reviewer.md in Claude Code
Program Your own code that calls a model with tools in a loop. Claude Code and Copilot are programs like this “I built my first agent” Claude Agent SDK, GitHub Copilot SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain

Most of the time, “an agent” means a session. Where it runs does not matter. A chat in VS Code and a window in the terminal are both agents if the AI may edit files and run commands by itself. If it can only answer, it is a chat.

Terminal or VS Code?

A session can run in a terminal window or in the VS Code extension. No survey counts how many people use each. What exists are descriptions from experienced engineers and from the companies themselves:

These are descriptions, not measurements.
Who Setup Source
About 900 engineers in a 2026 survey “A terminal with Claude Code open to drive work, and an IDE also open to review changes made by the agent.” Described as a common setup Pragmatic Engineer, Mar 2026
Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code (Anthropic) Five Claude sessions in numbered terminal tabs, plus five to ten more in the browser at claude.ai/code Write-up of his post on X, Jan 2026
Thibault Sottiaux, engineering lead of Codex (OpenAI) Calls the IDE extension Codex’s “most successful surface” and recommends it to new users as “the lowest friction option” Cerebral Valley interview, Jan 2026

Recommended setup

  • For one task: run the agent in a terminal and review its changes in the editor. VS Code’s built-in terminal puts both in one window. The extension works just as well: it is the same agent.
  • For long tasks on a remote server: run claude, copilot or codex inside tmux, a program that keeps terminal sessions running on the server. With Copilot, VS Code’s chat also works: start a new chat and set Session Target to Copilot, and it keeps working when the connection drops.
  • For several tasks at once: run several sessions, for example one per terminal tab or one per new chat. Give each session its own copy of the code (a git worktree), so they don’t change the same files. VS Code’s Agents window can set this up for you.

item.title: Free Local Dictation That Works Everywhere
item.description:
Part 1 of 2 · AI in my workflow
  1. Free Local Dictation That Works Everywhere
  2. AI Coding Agents in Practice: Claude Code, Copilot and Codex
TipTL;DR
  • Handy is the top free, offline dictation app. Install it from handy.computer.
  • In its settings, choose the Whisper large-v3-turbo model and an unused shortcut key, for example Caps Lock.

The problem

Working with AI tools means a lot of typing: in chat apps, coding assistants, the browser and the terminal. For long prompts, speaking is faster than typing. But the existing dictation options each have a problem.

Dictation inside AI apps only works in that app. The dictation in Claude and ChatGPT is very good, but it only works inside those apps, and not always there either. For example, it doesn’t work in the Claude Code extension for VS Code when VS Code is connected to a remote machine over SSH. The GitHub Copilot app also has its own dictation, but it uses a fixed model that you can’t change: NVIDIA’s nemotron-speech-streaming-en-0.6b, a small English-only model that runs on your own computer.

Dictation that works everywhere is weaker. Windows voice typing (Win + H) works in every app, but it makes many more mistakes than the dictation in the AI apps. It sends your audio to Microsoft’s cloud speech service, and Microsoft doesn’t say which model it uses.

The goal is one dictation tool for the whole computer that types into whatever window is active. It should also be free, with no subscription and no word limit.

Such a tool has two parts: the app handles the shortcut key, records your voice and pastes the text, and the model turns the speech into text.

Handy: free, offline, open source

Handy is a free, open-source app (MIT license) for Windows, macOS and Linux. You hold a shortcut key, speak, and release it. Handy then pastes the text where the cursor is. Everything runs on your own computer, and you choose the model. Pick a shortcut key that other apps don’t already use, for example Caps Lock.

Among the free, open-source apps for Windows, Handy is by far the most popular:

Star counts on 7 November 2026. Stars only give a rough idea of popularity.
App GitHub stars License First release
Handy 37,865 MIT Jun 2025
OpenWhispr 10,910 MIT Jul 2025
CapsWriter-Offline 7,083 MIT May 2023
Whispering (Epicenter) 4,840 unclear Mar 20231
Amical 1,599 MIT Jul 2025

Handy lets you choose between several models. The main ones:

Size in billions of parameters. Parakeet scores best on English benchmarks, but test both Whisper and Parakeet on your own voice.
Model Made by Size First release Languages Good for
Whisper large-v3-turbo OpenAI 0.8B Oct 2024 About 99, incl. Norwegian and Vietnamese Accents and many languages. Best with a GPU
Whisper large-v3 OpenAI 1.6B Nov 2023 About 99, incl. Norwegian and Vietnamese Slightly more accurate than turbo, but much slower
Parakeet V3 NVIDIA 0.6B Aug 2025 25 European Fast English, even on a CPU
Nemotron Streaming 3.5 NVIDIA 0.6B Jun 2026 32, incl. Norwegian and Vietnamese Live text while you speak, but less accurate
Voxtral Mini 3B Mistral 3B Jul 2025 8 major ones, incl. English Highest accuracy grade in Handy, but slower and needs more memory

The best-known dictation app, Wispr Flow, runs in the cloud and is not fully free. Its results often feel better than the models in Handy because it also cleans up the text with AI, but the free plan allows only about 2,000 words a week (after that it slows down, with a hard limit at 5,000 words).2 Since both apps work the same way, one option is to use Wispr Flow until the limit, then switch to Handy.

Does Handy really use the GPU?

The test machine is a laptop with two GPUs: a built-in Intel GPU and an NVIDIA RTX PRO 500 (6 GB memory, 40 W). handy.exe shows up in nvidia-smi, but that only means the app draws its window on the GPU. To check if the model itself runs on the GPU, measure the GPU once per second while dictating:

1..75 | % { nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv,noheader; Start-Sleep 1 }

The results show a clear pattern:

  • While speaking: the GPU is at 0% and uses 0 MiB of memory. Handy only records.
  • After releasing the key: the GPU works at 91% for about 1 second, and memory goes from 0 to about 1 GB. This is the model loading and transcribing.
  • A little later: the memory is free again, because Handy unloads the model when it isn’t in use.

Good to know about speed and memory:

  • “Speed” is the waiting time after you stop talking. Whisper-type models transcribe the whole recording in one go. On this GPU the wait is about one second, which feels instant.
  • Model size decides the memory use, not the length of the recording. Speaking longer takes more time, not more memory.
  • Bigger models fit in memory, but they are slower. Handy rates Mistral’s Voxtral Mini 3B better for English. It is about three times bigger, so each phrase could take around 3–4 seconds on this GPU. This is an estimate and hasn’t been measured yet.

Recommended setup

Handy with Whisper large-v3-turbo on an NVIDIA GPU: free, offline, no word limit, about one second per phrase, and it works in every app. The text is less polished than Wispr Flow’s, but for prompts to an AI it is good enough.

Footnotes

  1. This date is for the whole Epicenter repository, which contains more than Whispering. Whispering itself was launched on Hacker News in August 2025.↩︎

  2. From Wispr Flow’s documentation in November 2026. The limits can change at any time.↩︎
